newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court-martial prosecution in closing argument.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court-martial prosecution in closing argument.

text.p: The prosecutor in the court-martial of an Army drill sergeant said in closing arguments Thursday the accused used fear and intimidation to rape trainees under his command.

"The accused used his power as a drill sergeant and his easy access to trainees and his ability to control them in order to rape six different trainees over a 20-month period," prosecutor Capt. Theresa Gallagher said in her closing statement to the six-member military jury.

"He created an environment of fear, intimidation, and control," she said, describing Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson as an "unscrupulous drill sergeant grossly misusing his post to force his sexual attention on trainees."

Simpson, 32, is the first of 12 trainers charged in a sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground to go to trial, although four cases have been resolved through administrative means or plea agreements. He faces 19 charges of rape and 35 other related counts.

His lawyers have argued any sexual relationships he had were consensual. But Gallagher described in explicit detail in her statement the prosecution's version of how each of the six women was allegedly raped by Simpson.

She said he became increasingly aggressive and forceful in his pursuit of sex with trainees during his time at Aberdeen. "He becomes more perverted, more aggressive, more demanding over time as he becomes more experienced and more comfortable in his role as a drill sergeant," she said.

Simpson has pleaded innocent to rape and the other charges but earlier pleaded guilty to 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five of propositioning. He faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted of rape and a total of 32 years, dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the counts to which he has pleaded guilty.
In earlier court arguments, Simpson's lawyer Frank Spinner said the women who testified against him were not telling the truth in order "to get themselves out of trouble and get him in trouble."
Testimony in the trial ended Tuesday after eight days.
